subject: Latent variable with a shifted data

messages.author: cb9b7d5d2f1259a3
messages.subject: Latent variable with a shifted data
parts:
Hi all,

I am wondering if someone can help me to understand why a latent variable with two factors T1 and T2 (T1 has a factor loading equal to 1) gives me the same results when we shift T2 up by 10 units.
T2 is a scale which originally was from 2-38, but we realized that the correct scores are from 12-48. So all the scores were shifted 10 units up. But the CFA output is the same for both the original and shifted score. The code is as follows:

model1 <- '

              # Latent Variables

              X =~ 1*T1 + T2'
             
     CFAModel1<- lavaan::cfa(model=model1, data=Data, std.lv=TRUE)  
     lavaan:::summary(CFAModel1, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)

## T2_new is the T2 scale shifted up 10 units

model2 <- '

              # Latent Variables

              X =~ 1*T1 + T2_new'
             
     CFAModel2<- lavaan::cfa(model=model2, data=Data, std.lv=TRUE)  
     lavaan:::summary(CFAModel2, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)


I appreciate your help and time.

Farideh

messages.subject: Re: Latent variable with a shifted data
parts: why a latent variable with two factors T1 and T2 (T1 has a factor loading equal to 1) gives me the same results when we shift T2 up by 10 units.

Adding a constant changes the mean, but does not change a variable's correlation with any other variable.

x <- rnorm(10)
y <- rnorm(10)
cor(data.frame(x, y, y2 = y + 10))

             x           y          y2
x   1.00000000 -0.06841827 -0.06841827
y  -0.06841827  1.00000000  1.00000000
y2 -0.06841827  1.00000000  1.00000000

messages.subject: Re: Latent variable with a shifted data
parts:
On 1/18/23 16:55, Farideh Tavangar wrote:
> I am wondering if someone can help me to understand why a latent
> variable with two factors T1 and T2 (T1 has a factor loading equal to 1)
> gives me the same results when we shift T2 up by 10 units.

A constant shift only impacts the mean, not the factor loading. Think of
correlation: the correlation between a and b is the same as the
correlation between (a+10) and b.

Yves.
